breakfast.name: Cornetto e Cappuccino
instructions: Warm cornetto
Steam milk for cappuccino
breakfast.description: The Italian breakfast — cornetto and cappuccino.

breakfast.name: Fette Biscottate (Rusks)
instructions: Spread rusks with butter and jam
breakfast.description: Crunchy twice-baked bread with jam — typical Roman breakfast.

imageCredit.author: No machine-readable author provided. Rainer Zenz assumed (based on copyright claims).

breakfast.name: Cornetto e Cappuccino (Italian Breakfast)
ingredients: Cornetto (Italian croissant -- lighter and less buttery than French)
instructions: The Italian breakfast is famously simple: a cornetto and a cappuccino, standing at the bar
The cornetto: lighter than a French croissant, often filled with cream, jam, or Nutella
Cappuccino: espresso with steamed, frothed milk -- ONLY drunk in the morning in Italy
Ordering a cappuccino after 11 AM or after a meal is a well-known Italian faux pas
The bar (cafe counter): Italians stand at the bar, drink quickly, and leave -- sitting costs more
Vatican workers, Swiss Guards, and clergy all start the day this way
This breakfast applies to Vatican City because the Vatican is fully within Rome
breakfast.description: The universal Italian breakfast -- cornetto (lighter Italian croissant) and cappuccino (espresso with steamed milk foam), standing at the bar. Cappuccino is ONLY drunk before 11 AM in Italy -- ordering it later is a faux pas. Vatican workers, Swiss Guards, and clergy all start the day this way.

breakfast.name: Maritozzo (Roman Cream Bun)
ingredients: Brioche dough (flour, yeast, eggs, butter, sugar, orange zest)
instructions: Maritozzo is the Roman cream-filled brioche bun -- a breakfast and dessert icon
A soft, slightly sweet brioche bun sliced open and stuffed with whipped cream
The cream: overflowing, generous, cloud-like
An ancient Roman pastry -- the name may come from "marito" (husband) -- a gift from suitors
Nearly disappeared in the mid-20th century but has been revived in Roman bakeries
Now one of Rome's most Instagrammed foods
Eaten at breakfast or as an afternoon treat
breakfast.description: Roman cream bun -- maritozzo, soft brioche sliced open and overflowing with whipped cream. An ancient Roman pastry (the name may come from "marito" -- husband -- a suitor's gift). Nearly disappeared but revived in Roman bakeries. Now one of Rome's most Instagrammed foods.

lunch.name: Cacio e Pepe
instructions: Cook pasta, save starchy water
Toast pepper, add water to make cream
Toss with pasta
Fold in pecorino off heat until creamy
lunch.description: The Roman trinity of pasta, pecorino, and pepper.

lunch.name: Saltimbocca alla Romana
instructions: Press prosciutto and sage onto veal with toothpick
Fry in butter sage-side down
Flip, add wine
Serve immediately
lunch.description: 'Jump in the mouth' — veal with prosciutto and sage.

lunch.name: Cacio e Pepe (Cheese and Pepper Pasta)
ingredients: Pecorino Romano (sheep's milk cheese -- finely grated, generous)
Black pepper (coarsely ground, toasted in the pan)
instructions: Cacio e pepe is the most iconic Roman pasta -- just cheese, pepper, and pasta
Only three ingredients -- but the technique is everything
The challenge: creating a creamy sauce from cheese and pasta water without the cheese clumping
The starchy pasta water: the key -- it emulsifies the melting cheese into a smooth cream
Pecorino Romano: a sharp, salty sheep's milk cheese -- THE Roman cheese
Toasting the black pepper in the pan blooms its oils and reduces its raw bite
The simplicity is deceptive -- restaurants struggle with this dish more than complex ones
One of the four great Roman pastas (cacio e pepe, carbonara, amatriciana, gricia)
lunch.description: The most iconic Roman pasta -- cacio e pepe, just pecorino Romano, black pepper, and pasta. Three ingredients, but the technique is everything: starchy pasta water emulsifies the cheese into a cream without clumping. One of the four great Roman pastas. Deceptively difficult.

lunch.name: Pasta alla Carbonara
ingredients: Guanciale (cured pork jowl -- NOT bacon, NOT pancetta)
instructions: Carbonara is the Roman pasta that the world loves -- and the world makes wrong
The rules: guanciale (NOT bacon), pecorino (NOT parmesan), NO cream, NO garlic, NO onion
Guanciale: cured pork jowl -- fattier, more flavorful, and silkier than pancetta or bacon
The sauce: egg yolks mixed with pecorino, tempered by hot pasta -- a creamy custard, NOT scrambled eggs
The technique: the pan must be OFF the heat when the egg mixture is added -- too hot and the eggs scramble
Origin debated: possibly invented by Italian charcoal workers (carbonari), or post-WWII using American bacon and egg rations
The internet arguments about "authentic" carbonara are legendary
Adding cream to carbonara is the fastest way to anger an Italian
lunch.description: Rome's most famous pasta -- carbonara, guanciale (cured pork jowl, NOT bacon) rendered crispy, tossed with pasta, then egg yolks and pecorino Romano added OFF the heat to create a creamy custard (NOT scrambled eggs, NEVER cream). Origin debated: charcoal workers or WWII rations. Adding cream will anger every Italian.

lunch.name: Supplì (Roman Fried Rice Balls)
ingredients: Risotto (made with tomato sauce and ground beef)
instructions: Supplì are the Roman fried rice balls -- a street food and pizzeria appetizer
Rice cooked in tomato sauce (like a risotto), cooled, formed into oval balls
A cube of mozzarella hidden in the center
Breaded and fried until the outside is crispy and the mozzarella melts into a string
Called "supplì al telefono" because the melted mozzarella stretches like a telephone cord when pulled apart
Different from Sicilian arancini: supplì are oval, arancini are round; supplì are tomato-based, arancini vary
Sold at every pizzeria in Rome as an appetizer while you wait for your pizza
lunch.description: Roman fried rice balls -- supplì, tomato risotto with a hidden cube of mozzarella, breaded and fried. Called "supplì al telefono" because the melted mozzarella stretches like a telephone cord. Different from Sicilian arancini (oval vs round, tomato vs varied). Every Roman pizzeria's appetizer.

lunch.name: Saltimbocca alla Romana
instructions: Saltimbocca means "jump in the mouth" -- that's how good it is
Thin veal scallops topped with prosciutto and sage, pan-fried in butter
The sage leaf is pressed between the veal and prosciutto -- secured with a toothpick
Deglazed with white wine to create a quick pan sauce
A Roman classic -- quick, elegant, and intensely flavorful
The combination of sage, prosciutto, and butter is a Roman flavor signature
lunch.description: Roman classic -- saltimbocca alla Romana (jump in the mouth), thin veal with prosciutto and sage pan-fried in butter and deglazed with white wine. Quick and elegant. The sage-prosciutto-butter combination is a Roman flavor signature.

lunch.name: Trippa alla Romana (Roman Tripe)
instructions: Trippa alla Romana is Roman-style tripe -- a quinto quarto (fifth quarter) dish
Tripe: stomach lining -- the working-class protein of old Rome
Simmered in tomato sauce with a soffritto base
The defining herb: mentuccia (wild Roman mint) -- not regular mint
Finished with generous pecorino Romano
Traditionally eaten on Saturdays in Rome -- "trippa del sabato"
Part of the Roman tradition of offal cooking that also includes coda alla vaccinara and pajata
lunch.description: Roman tripe -- trippa alla Romana, tripe simmered in tomato sauce with mentuccia (wild Roman mint -- not regular mint) and finished with pecorino. The quinto quarto (fifth quarter) tradition. Eaten on Saturdays in Rome -- trippa del sabato.

dinner.name: Supplì (Rice Croquettes)
instructions: Roll risotto around mozzarella cube
Coat in egg and breadcrumbs
Deep fry until golden
Mozzarella should stretch when you break it
dinner.description: Roman rice croquettes with stretchy mozzarella center.

dinner.name: Abbacchio a Scottadito (Grilled Lamb Chops)
instructions: Marinate chops with rosemary, garlic, oil
Grill over high heat 3 min per side
Squeeze lemon, serve hot
dinner.description: 'Burn your fingers' lamb chops — eaten by hand while still hot.

dinner.name: Abbacchio alla Scottadito (Grilled Lamb Chops)
ingredients: Lamb rib chops (abbacchio -- young milk-fed lamb)
instructions: Abbacchio alla scottadito -- "burn your fingers" lamb chops
The name: the chops are eaten with your fingers, straight from the grill, so hot they burn
Abbacchio: young, milk-fed lamb -- a Roman specialty, especially at Easter
Marinated in olive oil, garlic, and rosemary, then grilled hot and fast
Squeezed with lemon at the table
Easter lamb is the most important Roman holiday food tradition
The Roman countryside (Lazio) is sheep country -- lamb and pecorino are the regional proteins
dinner.description: Roman grilled lamb -- abbacchio alla scottadito (burn your fingers), young milk-fed lamb chops marinated in olive oil, garlic, and rosemary, grilled hot. Eaten with your fingers, so hot they burn. Easter lamb is Rome's most important holiday food. Lazio is sheep country.

dinner.name: Pasta all'Amatriciana
ingredients: San Marzano tomatoes (or good canned plum tomatoes)
instructions: Amatriciana is the Roman tomato pasta -- from the town of Amatrice in Lazio
The third of the four great Roman pastas (cacio e pepe, carbonara, amatriciana, gricia)
Guanciale rendered crispy, tomato sauce added, tossed with bucatini, finished with pecorino
Bucatini: thick hollow spaghetti -- the sauce gets inside the tube
A slight chili heat from peperoncino
After the 2016 Amatrice earthquake, "amatriciana" became a solidarity dish -- restaurants donated proceeds
The debate: some add onion, but purists say absolutely not
dinner.description: Roman tomato pasta from Amatrice -- amatriciana, guanciale rendered crispy, San Marzano tomato sauce, bucatini (hollow spaghetti -- sauce gets inside), finished with pecorino and peperoncino. After the 2016 Amatrice earthquake, it became a solidarity dish. Third of the four great Roman pastas.

dinner.name: Coda alla Vaccinara (Oxtail Stew)
ingredients: Oxtail (cut into segments at the joints)
Pine nuts, raisins, cocoa powder (the sweet-savory finish -- traditional)
instructions: Coda alla vaccinara is the Roman oxtail stew -- the dish of the Roman slaughterhouse workers
Vaccinari: the cattle workers of the Testaccio slaughterhouse district in Rome
They were paid partly in offcuts (the "quinto quarto" -- the fifth quarter: offal, tail, tripe)
Oxtail braised for 3+ hours until the meat falls off the bone and the collagen melts
The celery: an unusually large amount is used -- it defines the dish
The sweet finish: pine nuts, raisins, and a touch of cocoa powder
Cucina povera (poor cooking) at its finest -- turning the cheapest cut into the richest dish
Roman working-class food elevated to restaurant standard
dinner.description: Roman slaughterhouse workers' dish -- coda alla vaccinara, oxtail braised 3+ hours until collagen-melted, with lots of celery, tomato, and a sweet-savory finish (pine nuts, raisins, cocoa). The vaccinari (cattle workers of Testaccio) were paid in offcuts -- the "quinto quarto" (fifth quarter). Cucina povera: cheapest cut, richest dish.

dinner.name: Pasta alla Gricia
instructions: Gricia is the fourth of the four great Roman pastas -- and the ancestor of the others
Guanciale and pecorino with pasta -- no egg (that's carbonara) and no tomato (that's amatriciana)
Considered the "grandmother" of the Roman pasta family -- the simplest form
The guanciale fat renders and coats the pasta, emulsified with pasta water and pecorino
Less famous than carbonara and amatriciana, but Roman purists often consider it the best
Named after the town of Grisciano in Lazio
dinner.description: The fourth great Roman pasta and ancestor of the others -- gricia, guanciale and pecorino with pasta (no egg = not carbonara, no tomato = not amatriciana). The "grandmother" of the family. Roman purists often consider it the best. Named after Grisciano in Lazio.

dinner.name: Vignarola (Roman Spring Vegetable Stew)
instructions: Vignarola is the Roman spring vegetable stew -- a celebration of the season
Made only in spring when fava beans, artichokes, and peas are all in season simultaneously
The window: March through May -- after that, the dish is out of season
A dish that enforces seasonality -- you cannot make proper vignarola in winter
The Roman artichoke (carciofo romanesco): a large, thornless globe artichoke, tender enough to eat raw
Italian cooking philosophy: eat what is in season, locally, and simply prepared
dinner.description: Roman spring stew -- vignarola, fresh fava beans, artichokes, and peas cooked with guanciale, olive oil, and mint. Made ONLY in spring (March-May) when all three are in season simultaneously. A dish that enforces Italian seasonality: you cannot make proper vignarola in winter.

snacks.name: Pizza Bianca
instructions: Stretch dough, dimple with fingers
Drizzle with olive oil and salt
Add rosemary
Bake at 250°C until golden
snacks.description: Roman white pizza — just olive oil and salt.

snacks.name: Pizza al Taglio (Roman Sliced Pizza)
ingredients: Toppings: endless variety -- potato and rosemary, zucchini flower, mortadella
instructions: Pizza al taglio is Roman sliced pizza -- sold by weight, cut with scissors
Baked in large rectangular trays (teglia)
The dough: high-hydration, fermented 24-48 hours -- light, airy, and digestible
You point to what you want, the pizzaiolo cuts it with scissors, and you pay by weight
Unlike Neapolitan pizza (round, wood-fired, eaten sitting), Roman pizza al taglio is grab-and-go
Toppings change throughout the day -- morning: simple (potato, margherita). Lunch: elaborate
The Roman way to eat pizza is on the street, walking
snacks.description: Roman sliced pizza -- pizza al taglio, baked in rectangular trays, cut with scissors, sold by weight. High-hydration dough fermented 24-48 hours. Grab-and-go street food (unlike sit-down Neapolitan pizza). Toppings change throughout the day. The Roman way to eat pizza is walking.

snacks.name: Fiori di Zucca Fritti (Fried Zucchini Flowers)
ingredients: Filling: mozzarella and anchovy (one of each inside the flower)
Light batter: flour, water (or sparkling water), salt
instructions: Fried zucchini flowers are a Roman summer delicacy
Fresh zucchini flowers stuffed with a piece of mozzarella and a single anchovy fillet
Dipped in a light batter and deep-fried until golden and crispy
The flower opens in the hot oil -- the mozzarella melts inside
A seasonal dish -- only when zucchini are flowering (late spring through summer)
The mozzarella-anchovy combination: creamy and salty
snacks.description: Roman summer delicacy -- fiori di zucca fritti, fresh zucchini flowers stuffed with mozzarella and anchovy, battered and fried. The flower opens in hot oil, the mozzarella melts inside. Seasonal (late spring through summer). Creamy and salty combination.

snacks.name: Porchetta (Slow-Roasted Pork)
ingredients: Wild fennel (finocchietto selvatico -- the essential herb)
instructions: Porchetta is the slow-roasted, herbed whole pig -- a Lazio and central Italian tradition
A whole pig is deboned, seasoned inside with wild fennel, garlic, and rosemary
Rolled, tied, and slow-roasted for 4-8 hours until the skin is crackling-crispy
Wild fennel (finocchietto selvatico): the defining herb -- anise-like, herby, and aromatic
Sold from vans and trucks at markets, festivals, and roadsides across Lazio
Sliced thick and served in a bread roll -- the porchetta sandwich
The city of Ariccia (near Rome) claims the best porchetta in the world
The crispy skin (crosta) is the most prized part
snacks.description: Lazio slow-roasted whole pig -- porchetta, deboned pig seasoned with wild fennel, garlic, and rosemary, roasted 4-8 hours until skin is crackling. Sold from vans at markets. Ariccia (near Rome) claims the best. The crispy skin (crosta) is the most prized part. Served in a bread roll.

snacks.name: Tramezzino (Italian Tea Sandwich)
ingredients: Fillings: tuna and artichoke, prosciutto and mozzarella, egg salad, salmon and arugula
instructions: Tramezzini are the Italian soft white bread sandwiches -- triangular, crustless
Found at every bar (cafe) in Rome alongside the cornetti
Filled with Italian ingredients: tuna-artichoke, prosciutto-mozzarella, salmon-arugula
Soft white bread -- the opposite of crusty Italian bread
A quick lunch or snack -- eaten at the bar with an espresso
Invented in Turin in the 1920s -- the name comes from the poet D'Annunzio
snacks.description: Italian soft sandwich -- tramezzino, crustless white bread triangles with fillings like tuna-artichoke or prosciutto-mozzarella. Found at every Roman bar (cafe). Invented in Turin (1920s), named by poet D'Annunzio. Quick lunch eaten standing at the bar with an espresso.

desserts.name: Maritozzo (Cream Bun)
instructions: Make sweet brioche buns, bake
Cool, split open
Fill generously with whipped cream
Dust with powdered sugar
desserts.description: Sweet Roman bun overstuffed with whipped cream.

desserts.name: Tiramisu
instructions: Tiramisu is the most famous Italian dessert -- its origin is fiercely contested
The name: "tira mi su" means "pick me up" or "lift me up"
Ladyfingers dipped in espresso, layered with mascarpone cream, dusted with cocoa
No baking required -- it sets in the refrigerator
The mascarpone cream: egg yolks beaten with sugar until thick, then folded with mascarpone
Claimed by the Veneto (Treviso) and Friuli-Venezia Giulia regions -- not Roman, but eaten everywhere in Rome
The Vatican cafeteria surely serves it -- it is ubiquitous in Roman restaurants
desserts.description: Italy's most famous dessert -- tiramisu (pick me up), ladyfingers dipped in espresso, layered with mascarpone cream, dusted with cocoa. No baking. Origin contested between Veneto and Friuli. Ubiquitous in Roman restaurants and certainly in Vatican cafeterias.

desserts.name: Crostata (Italian Jam Tart)
ingredients: Pasta frolla (Italian shortcrust: flour, butter, sugar, egg yolks, lemon zest)
Jam filling: apricot, cherry, or mixed berry (homemade or quality)
Lattice strips of dough on top
instructions: Crostata is the Italian jam tart -- the most classic Roman home dessert
Pasta frolla: the Italian sweet shortcrust -- richer and more crumbly than French pate sucree
Filled with jam and topped with a lattice of dough strips
Every Italian grandmother (nonna) makes crostata -- it is THE home baking standard
The lattice: strips of dough laid in a cross-hatch pattern -- simple but decorative
Apricot jam (marmellata di albicocche) is the most traditional filling
Served at breakfast, merenda (afternoon snack), or as dessert
desserts.description: The Italian nonna's home dessert -- crostata, pasta frolla (rich shortcrust with lemon zest) filled with jam (apricot most traditional) and topped with lattice strips. Every Italian grandmother makes crostata. The home baking standard. Served at breakfast, merenda, or dessert.

desserts.name: Panna Cotta
ingredients: Gelatin (just enough to set -- it should wobble)
Berry coulis or caramel sauce (for serving)
instructions: Panna cotta is the Italian set cream dessert -- "cooked cream"
Cream heated with sugar and vanilla, set with a minimal amount of gelatin
The key: it should WOBBLE -- barely set, trembling like custard
Too much gelatin and it becomes rubbery -- the restraint is the skill
Served turned out of a mold with berry coulis or caramel
Originally from Piedmont but served across Italy, including Rome
desserts.description: Italian set cream -- panna cotta (cooked cream), cream heated with vanilla and set with minimal gelatin. Must WOBBLE -- barely set and trembling. Too much gelatin makes it rubbery: the restraint is the skill. Served with berry coulis or caramel.

desserts.name: Gelato
ingredients: Egg yolks (for custard-based flavors like stracciatella, pistachio)
Flavoring: vanilla bean, pistachios from Bronte, hazelnut paste, fresh fruit, chocolate
instructions: Gelato is the Italian ice cream -- denser, smoother, and more intensely flavored than American ice cream
Less air (overrun) churned in -- denser and creamier
Lower fat than American ice cream -- the flavor comes from the ingredients, not from fat
Served at a slightly warmer temperature -- softer, more scoopable
The best gelaterias in Rome: Fatamorgana, Giolitti (since 1900), Come il Latte
Pistachio: the flagship flavor -- made with pistachios from Bronte, Sicily
The sign of bad gelato: neon colors and mountains piled above the tub
Good gelato is stored flat in covered pans -- not piled in pyramids
A post-dinner passeggiata (evening walk) tradition: walking through Rome with a gelato cone
desserts.description: Italian ice cream -- gelato, denser and smoother than American (less air, lower fat, warmer serving temperature). The best sign: stored flat in covered pans, not piled in neon pyramids. Pistachio from Bronte, Sicily is the flagship. A post-dinner passeggiata tradition: walking through Rome with a cone.

drinks.name: Espresso
instructions: Pull a shot from machine or moka pot
Serve in small cup
drinks.description: A quick, intense shot — the Italian way.

drinks.name: Frascati Wine
instructions: Serve chilled
From the hills south of Rome
drinks.description: Crisp white wine from the Castelli Romani.

drinks.name: Espresso
ingredients: Water (pressurized through the grounds at 9 bars of pressure)
Served in a small ceramic cup (tazzina)
instructions: Espresso is the Italian coffee -- and the Vatican runs on it
A shot of intensely concentrated coffee extracted under pressure
Drunk standing at the bar, quickly -- not lingered over
The crema: the golden-brown foam on top -- a sign of good extraction
After lunch, after dinner, mid-morning, mid-afternoon -- Italians drink espresso all day
But NEVER cappuccino after 11 AM -- espresso only
The bar (cafe) is a social institution -- a brief moment of pleasure in the workday
drinks.description: The fuel of Italy and the Vatican -- espresso, concentrated coffee extracted under 9 bars of pressure. Drunk standing at the bar, quickly. The crema (golden foam) signals good extraction. Italians drink espresso all day, but NEVER cappuccino after 11 AM.

drinks.name: Aperol Spritz
instructions: The Aperol Spritz is the Italian aperitivo drink -- the golden-orange glass in every Roman piazza
The ritual of aperitivo: a pre-dinner drink with small bites, usually around 6-8 PM
Aperol: a bitter orange liqueur from Padova -- lighter and sweeter than Campari
The ratio: 3 parts Prosecco, 2 parts Aperol, 1 splash soda -- over ice with an orange slice
The Spritz has become globally ubiquitous -- but in Rome it's part of the daily rhythm
The aperitivo is not just a drink -- it's a social ritual marking the transition from work to evening
drinks.description: Italian aperitivo ritual -- Aperol Spritz, Aperol (bitter orange liqueur), Prosecco, and a splash of soda over ice. The golden-orange glass in every Roman piazza at 6-8 PM. The aperitivo marks the transition from work to evening -- a social ritual, not just a drink.
